meta.title: Memetic Co-design of 2D Locomotion at Variable Gravity
meta.authorsHtml: Leone Costi<sup>∗</sup><sup>1</sup>, Leon Williams<sup>1</sup>, Dario Izzo<sup>1</sup>

abstract: Designing robots capable of efficient locomotion requires an embodied approach that tightly couples morphology, control, and environmental interaction. This challenge is particularly critical for planetary exploration, where robotic systems must autonomously adapt to diverse gravitational regimes and unstructured terrains. In this work, we present a memetic co-design framework that combines evolutionary search over robot body morphology with gradient-based optimization of actuation parameters. Using this framework, we show how gravitational acceleration influences the co-evolution of morphology and locomotion strategies. Experiments conducted across multiple gravity settings demonstrate that the proposed approach can autonomously identify transitions between distinct locomotion regimes, revealing how environmental conditions shape embodied behavior. This ability suggests that applying the framework to more detailed robotic simulations may expose critical morphological and control adaptations relevant to real planetary operations.

blocks.html: Designing robots capable of efficient locomotion requires tightly coupling morphology and control [1, 2]. Although traditional robotics tends to address these challenges separately, co-design can jointly optimize a robot’s physical structure and control policy, enabling the discovery of locomotion strategies that emerge from their interaction [3–5]. Space exploration in particular represents a clear application in which co-design is fundamental: robots deployed on planetary bodies must operate within strict constraints and no servicing [6, 7]. Design choices that appear interchangeable under Earth gravity may become decisive under different gravitational conditions [8, 9]. Therefore, treating gravity as an explicit design variable enables systematic mapping from environmental conditions to robot morphology and gait strategies, revealing locomotion regimes that differ significantly between destinations [10–14].

Evolutionary robotics has demonstrated that robot bodies and controllers can be evolved simultaneously [1, 15, 16] and have been implemented for space exploration [17]. However, it often requires a very large number of simulation evaluations due to the combinatorial complexity of morphology–control search spaces [18, 19].

Differentiable physics simulation enables gradient-based optimization through physical dynamics [20–22]. However, whereas it offers a quicker way to obtain optimal control, it lacks the freedom to arbitrarily define sudden morphological changes, preventing the emergence of the wide range of morphologies and locomotion gaits that have been observed and manually designed for different gravity regimes [23, 24].

All in all, gradient-based methods may converge to local optima, while purely evolutionary approaches that can better explore vastly different strategies may converge slowly [25–27]. Hybrid approaches combining evolutionary exploration with gradient-based refinement, often described as memetic optimization, offer a promising balance between global exploration and local exploitation [28–30].

In this work, we present a memetic co-design framework for locomotion systems that integrates evolutionary morphology search with gradient-based optimization [31–33]. This differs from purely evolutionary approaches [17], as the control is optimized through gradients, thus lowering the amount of parameters that need to be evolved, and increasing computational efficiency. We do so by presenting the simple model of locomotion on a flat rigid terrain. Such a choice allows us to keep the simulations efficient while investigating how environmental gravity affects the design of both morphology and control, thus showcasing the principle of embodiment during locomotion.

We developed a memetic computational pipeline for the automatic discovery of robotic designs using a combination of differentiable physics simulation and evolutionary search. The robots are modeled as squares of flexible active material. Whilst far from the complex design of a planetary rover, maintaining a simple simulation environment allows us to effectively investigate the proposed co-design tool and focus on the synergy between evolutionary and gradient-based approaches. We simulate locomotion a flat rigid plane with known environmental gravity. This is not a realistic scenario, as terrain features, inclines and even the value of gravity is likely not uniform and not necessarily known. However, such a simplification allows the simulation to be computationally efficient and to isolate the principles of the proposed memetic design.

The overall workflow proceeds as illustrated in Fig. 1. A population of candidates is generated using NEAT [34]. Each genome specifies the morphology of a specific individual. The robot is simulated in Taichi, where actuation parameters are refined via gradient-based optimization. The resulting locomotion performance determines the fitness of the genome, which is then used by the evolutionary algorithm to generate the next population. This hybrid optimization strategy combines the global exploration capabilities of evolutionary algorithms with the local optimization efficiency of gradient-based learning, achieving a co-design of morphology and actuation strategies.

blocks.caption: Schematics of the memetic co-design pipeline. NEAT is used to create a generation of robot morphologies. Each individual of the generation is then simulated in Taichi, and the control parameters are optimized to maximize forward displacement.
blocks.label: Figure

blocks.html: The physical behavior of the robots is simulated using a differentiable implementation of the material points method thanks to DiffTaichi [22]. This formulation allows us to compute and obtain gradients through the physical simulation.

In the present implementation, each lattice cell can assume one of five discrete material states: empty space or one of four actuator types. Empty cells correspond to regions of the domain that contain no particles. The remaining four material types correspond to independent actuators that expand periodically. Actuation is implemented by injecting an additional time-dependent deformation signal into particles belonging to actuator regions. This simple volumetric actuation has been chosen because it is characteristic of many actuators in soft robotics, including pneumatics [35].
Each actuator i ∈{0, . . . , 3} produces a vertical (along the local y-axis of the robot) periodic actuation signal defined as a displacement ai, as follows:

blocks.html: where wik are learnable weights, ωi denotes the actuation frequency of actuator i, and bi is a bias term controlling the baseline activation level and A is the maximum strength of the actuation. In our implementation, we set K = 4, corresponding to four sinusoidal basis functions with evenly distributed phase offsets over the oscillation cycle. This representation can be interpreted as a low-order Fourier expansion of the actuation signal, providing sufficient expressivity to generate a range of smooth periodic deformation patterns while keeping the dimensionality of the optimization problem small. Using a small set of sinusoidal basis functions encourages coordinated oscillatory behavior between actuators, which is observed in natural soft-bodied systems.
The controller parameters optimized during simulation are collected into a parameter vector:

This parameter vector is optimized using gradient descent within the differentiable simulation. Gradients of the locomotion loss with respect to θ are computed through automatic differentiation of the simulation dynamics, and parameters are updated using the Adam optimization algorithm.
The loss function measures the negative forward locomotion of the robot and is defined as the negative horizontal displacement of the robot’s center of mass over the simulation horizon:

where xCOM(t) denotes the horizontal position of the robot’s center of mass at time t and T is the final simulation time. Note this loss function is differentiable with respect to the control parameters thanks to DiffTaichi [22].

While actuator parameters are optimized using gradient descent within the differentiable simulator, the morphology of the robot is optimized using an evolutionary algorithm. Each genome encodes a neural network that maps spatial coordinates of lattice cells to one of the aforementioned five discrete material types, thus defining the morphology of the robot for that genome.

The evolutionary process begins with a population of simple neural networks with minimal connectivity. Over successive generations, networks are modified through mutation and crossover operators. Mutations can introduce new nodes or connections, modify connection weights, or remove existing structures. NEAT also employs speciation to group similar genomes, allowing novel topologies to emerge without immediate competition from highly optimized individuals.

During each generation, every genome in the population undergoes the following evaluation procedure: the genome is decoded into a neural network, which is queried over the robot lattice to generate a morphology, and for each morphology, the robot is simulated, and its control parameters are optimized using the aforementioned gradient-descent approach. Fitness is computed from the locomotion loss defined in Eq. (3), which measures the forward displacement of the robot during simulation.
The main NEAT parameters used in our experiments are summarized in Table 1. The morphologies generated at the first generation are shown in Fig. 2.

blocks.html: Evolution proceeds for a predefined number of generations, and the best-performing genome at the end of evolution defines the final robot morphology and the overall performance herein reported.

Locomotion is naturally affected by gravity. In this work, we are testing our pipeline under different gravity conditions, in order to showcase how the design of soft robots should differ according to the planet on which they are intended to be deployed. Fig. 3 illustrates individual cases of the changes between the first and last generation for the different tested values of gravity. Regardless of gravity, the first-generation individuals barely move, and instead, they mostly hop in place. This is to be expected as those individuals are completely randomized. Conversely, lastgeneration examples are shown to have developed effective strategies of forward locomotion. Noticeably, Fig. 3b and d clearly showcase ground clearance, indicating an areal gait, whereas Fig. 3f and h seem to indicate that a ground-bound rolling gait is preferred at high gravity.

Furthermore, Fig. 4 shows the morphologies generated by NEAT in the last generation for the case of g = 9.81 m/s2. It can be observed that such a generation does not contain any invalid design, as expected. Moreover, it can be seen that only one design includes empty space. We believe that this trend is driven by the absence of a mass-dependent term in the loss function, which would lead to more active material being selected, resulting in a larger volumetric actuation and thus more achieved displacement.

blocks.html: To characterize the evolution of the morphology, Fig. 5 shows how the fitness increases throughout the generations. It can be noticed that the performance quickly increases and reaches a plateau as early as generation 40. It is also clear that the proposed methodology effectively achieves locomotion across all tested gravity levels, as indicated by the fact that all tested conditions have the same trend and similar achieved fitness.

blocks.caption: Performance of the memetic co-design pipeline as a function of NEAT generations for the different tested gravity.
blocks.label: Figure

blocks.html: To further investigate how the proposed pipeline achieves similar performances across gravity whilst showcasing qualitatively different gaits (hopping and rolling), Fig. 6 shows the optimized frequencies of the actuators. Since the four actuators can be independently optimized by gradient descent, we have sorted them by increasing frequency, rather than by their IDs. Fig. 6a in particular shows the relationship between gravity and actuation frequency: lower gravities are characterized by higher frequencies, which decrease as gravity increases. This can be noticed by the 3rd ranked actuator, which on average decreases its frequency steadily going from Moon gravity (1.62 m/s2) to Earth gravity (9.81 m/s2). Moreover, Fig. 6b also shows that Earth gravity leads to a much more balanced split of the robot morphology between the four actuators, whereas up to Mars gravity (3.71 m/s2) the two higher frequency actuators are characterized by higher fractions. Even if the fraction corresponding to 0.2 m/s2 appears similar to the one for 9.81 m/s2, Fig. 6a shows that the actuators ranked 2nd and 3rd have on average a significantly higher frequency at 0.2 m/s2. We believe that this shift is the reason behind the observed change from hopping to rolling, as gravity increases. Lastly, it can be seen that in all cases the slowest actuator collapses to 0 Hz. This effectively makes it a passive element, showcasing that even if passive elements were not directly encoded in the memetic algorithm, their presence can arise by the gradient-descent converging to null frequency.

blocks.caption: Statistics about the four actuators, sorted and ranked by increasing frequency: (a) optimized frequency and (b) fraction of the morphology composed of each actuator. The four actuators are ranked from lowest to highest frequency rather than by their IDs.
blocks.label: Figure

blocks.html: The effect of the gradient-descent optimization is quantified in Fig. 7. It can be seen how, in the first generation, it is rarely possible to follow the gradients and increase the performance with respect to the initial NEAT guess. Conversely, the last generation shows a greater and consistent increase in fitness thanks to the optimization of control parameters. These results showcase how the memetic codesign manages to increase locomotion performances: because the gradient-descent loss and the genetic algorithm’s fitness are fundamentally the same function, generation after generation, NEAT is able to create morphologies that showcase a better gradient, which allows for a greater gradient-based performance increase.

blocks.caption: Effect of the gradient-descent control optimization on the performance as a function of the different tested gravity. First-generation mean data is reported in blue and last-generation mean in green.
blocks.label: Figure

blocks.html: The proposed memetic co-design of robots for space exploration discovers different locomotion regimes. With respect to previous works solely on the co-evolution of morphology and control at various gravity values, we have found a relation between environmental gravity and the airborne phase of the gait cycle. However, further investigation of our framework in 3D is needed before concluding that this phenomenon is induced by the gradient optimization. Our experiments highlight the role of gravity as a key factor shaping both morphology and locomotion strategies. Different gravitational regimes lead to distinct movement patterns and structural adaptations, balancing the different actuator types and lowering the actuation frequency, to change from aerial gaits to ground-bound ones as gravity increases.

However, all designs have evolved without any empty space, probably due to the absence of a mass-dependent or power-dependent term in the loss and fitness, thus always making it more favorable to add active material for more power. Moreover, experiments were conducted with a simplified simulation environment, and we endorse future work on 3D simulations with better actuation models, more complex mechanical designs, and uncertain terrain. Lastly, whereas abstract simulators are often used for soft matter and soft robots, it is clear that the gap from simulations to the manufacturing of such robots still has several challenges, and we endorse future work on the sim-to-real gap and on the potential manufacturing of the designed robots.
The source code used to run the simulations and obtain results can be found at https://gitlab.com/ EuropeanSpaceAgency/morph_optimization.
